_comment: Deterministic offline corpus for AgentFlow's demo scenario. Every document is synthetic: the text is written for this fixture set, the URLs are illustrative, and nothing here was retrieved from the live web. Fixture results are labelled as fixtures everywhere they surface and are never presented as live retrieval.

documents.title: Apache Airflow: scheduler architecture and operational profile
documents.excerpt: Apache Airflow schedules DAGs defined in Python and has the largest community of the open-source orchestrators. A deployment runs a scheduler, a metadata database, and one or more workers, which is a meaningful operational footprint for a small team. Its plugin ecosystem is extensive, and most data platforms publish an Airflow provider.

documents.title: Running Airflow with a two-person platform team
documents.excerpt: Teams of fewer than five engineers frequently report that Airflow's upgrade path and scheduler tuning consume more time than the pipelines themselves. Managed offerings reduce that burden but introduce per-task pricing that grows with schedule frequency.

documents.title: Prefect: dynamic flows and a lighter local story
documents.excerpt: Prefect models work as flows and tasks written in ordinary Python, with no static DAG declaration. Local execution needs only the library, which shortens the first-run experience considerably. Scheduling and observability are provided by a server component that teams either self-host or consume as a hosted service.

documents.title: Where Prefect's flexibility costs you
documents.excerpt: Because flows are ordinary Python, their structure is only known at runtime. That makes dynamic fan-out straightforward and static analysis harder: a change in control flow is not visible until a run executes it.

documents.title: Dagster: assets, typing and built-in testability
documents.excerpt: Dagster centres on software-defined assets rather than tasks, so a pipeline describes the data it produces instead of the steps it runs. Asset lineage and typed inputs and outputs are first-class, and the local development loop is explicitly designed around unit-testing individual assets.

documents.title: Adoption cost of the asset model
documents.excerpt: The asset abstraction is the main thing a team has to learn. Engineers accustomed to task graphs often need a week or two before the model feels natural, and migrating an existing task-oriented pipeline is a rewrite rather than a port.

documents.title: Operational burden compared across three orchestrators
documents.excerpt: Measured by the number of long-running components a team must keep healthy, Airflow has the heaviest self-hosted profile, Dagster sits in the middle with its daemon and web server, and Prefect is lightest for purely local use but converges with the others once a server is self-hosted.

documents.title: Testing stories compared
documents.excerpt: Dagster's asset functions are ordinary callables and test like any other function. Prefect flows are testable in-process. Airflow tasks are testable but commonly require a configured metadata database for anything involving the scheduler.

documents.title: Licensing and the open-core boundary
documents.excerpt: All three projects publish an Apache-2.0 core. Each also sells a hosted product, and the boundary between the open core and the paid offering differs: role-based access control and long-term run history are commonly on the paid side.

documents.title: Temporal is a different category
documents.excerpt: Temporal targets durable application workflows rather than scheduled data pipelines. Teams evaluating it alongside data orchestrators usually find the comparison does not hold: the failure model and the programming model are both different.

documents.title: Throughput notes (no methodology published)
documents.excerpt: Several blog posts circulate throughput figures for these schedulers. None of the ones surveyed here publish their hardware, task shape, or concurrency settings, so the numbers are not comparable and are reproduced nowhere in this corpus.
